Nothing read here compares people who use concentrates with people who do not use cannabis, follows anyone beyond one hour, or reports long-term, lung, dependence or mental-health results for concentrates.

A systematic review of observational studies searched to January 2021 (Petrilli et al., 2022; 20 articles from 16 studies by the editors' count, none rated good quality, no meta-analysis because every study relied on what people said they used and definitions of strength differed) found stronger cannabis (skunk-type, or types of 10% THC or more) associated with psychosis in two case-control studies and one cohort, all rated fair: against never-use, first-episode psychosis was more likely with skunk-type use in a UK study (adjusted odds ratio 2.91, 95% CI 1.52 to 3.60) and with types of 10% THC or more across six countries (1.6, 1.2 to 2.2; 4.8 with daily use), but not with hash-type or lower-strength use (0.83; 1.1), and relapse after a first episode was more likely with continued daily use of stronger cannabis (3.28, 1.22 to 9.18, against former use); none of these three studies looked at concentrates as a separate form. Findings for anxiety and depression varied. The studies of concentrates themselves were all cross-sectional and rated poor: in a 20-country online survey of 181,870 people, those who used butane hash oil more often reported a past diagnosis of anxiety (odds ratio 1.80, 1.60 to 2.01) or depression (1.34, 1.21 to 1.48) than those who used lower-strength herbal cannabis, but not of psychosis (1.11, 0.85 to 1.46); a US sample of 156 found no clear association of concentrate use with psychosis, anxiety or depression symptoms, and another of 191 no difference in anxiety or depression between people who frequently used concentrates and people who frequently used herbal cannabis; in a within-person survey of 574 people, mostly using infrequently, psychosis-like experiences were slightly less frequent with concentrates than with herbal cannabis (Cohen's d 0.12); and among 71 Japanese patients, liquid or resin forms went with less residual or late-onset psychosis than dry herbal cannabis (odds ratio 0.21, 0.06 to 0.74). The review's findings on strength and cannabis use disorder are set out in a separate claim. Its authors argue that people taking less of stronger products would weaken rather than inflate these associations, and that people with poorer mental health may choose stronger products. No study read here follows people who use concentrates beyond one hour, compares them with people who do not use cannabis, or reports lung or other long-term physical outcomes for concentrates.

set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Field study (Bidwell 2020): ROBINS-E overall high; confounding and selection each high (self-chosen form, groups differing in concentrate days, years of regular use and baseline THC metabolite; volunteers who had used the strongest product before; 12 people left out by their post-use blood THC), no placebo, thirteen outcomes tested at a fixed threshold, near-threshold results described inconsistently. Scoping review (Bero 2023): AMSTAR 2 critically low (provisional), mainly because it does not assess bias in the studies it maps; it extracts no results. Systematic review (Petrilli 2022): AMSTAR 2 low confidence (provisional; the list of excluded studies is in an appendix not read); none of its 16 studies was rated good, and its concentrate studies are cross-sectional and rated poor.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: One field study for the acute comparison; the scoping review reports no results to compare with it. For mental-health outcomes, the concentrate studies in the systematic review disagree with one another (more self-reported anxiety and depression diagnoses with butane hash oil in one survey, no clear association in two small US samples, slightly fewer psychosis-like experiences in a within-person survey, less chronic psychosis in a small clinical sample); they qualify the claim and do not change the rating of its acute finding.

evidence_add.extracted: Systematic review of observational studies: MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO from inception to 14 January 2021 with English search terms, plus reference lists; human observational studies comparing higher- with lower-potency cannabis as each study defined it, for depression, anxiety, psychosis or cannabis use disorder; experimental studies, conference abstracts, editorials and correspondence excluded; PROSPERO CRD42021226447. 4,171 titles screened, 89 full texts assessed, 20 articles included, printed as 20 studies with 119,581 participants (8 on psychosis, 8 anxiety, 7 depression, 6 cannabis use disorder); by the editors' count the tables hold 16 distinct studies (the GAP study in four articles, EU-GEI in two), and the printed participant total is smaller than one included survey (181,870). None was rated good on a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (editors' count: 5 fair, 11 poor). No meta-analysis was possible because exposure was self-reported, no precise measure of THC exposure was available and definitions of higher and lower potency differed.

Two case-control studies and one cohort, all rated fair. UK GAP study (410 patients with first-episode psychosis, 370 controls from the same area): against never-use, skunk-type use adjusted odds ratio 2.91 (95% CI 1.52 to 3.60), hash-type 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77), daily skunk-type use 5.40 (2.80 to 11.30); onset about 4 years earlier with higher-potency use (hazard ratio 1.68, 1.08 to 2.63). EU-GEI study (901 patients and 1,237 population controls in England, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain and Brazil): types of 10% THC or more against never-use 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2), under 10% 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5); daily use 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3) and 2.2 (1.4 to 3.6). Both adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, education, employment, tobacco, alcohol and other drugs. UK cohort of 256 patients after a first episode: 58% of those who continued daily use of higher-potency cannabis relapsed within 2 years against 24% of those who had used cannabis in the past (adjusted odds ratio 3.28, 1.22 to 9.18); lower-potency or infrequent higher-potency use 1.82 (0.36 to 8.75); adjusted for alcohol, other illicit drugs, cigarettes, care intensity at onset and medication adherence. None of these three studies looked at concentrates as a separate form.

Studies of concentrates, all cross-sectional and rated poor. 20-country online survey of 181,870 (self-report with pictorial aids; adjusted for age, gender, sexual orientation, education and other substance use), butane hash oil against lower-potency herbal cannabis: self-reported lifetime psychosis diagnosis 1.11 (0.85 to 1.46), anxiety diagnosis 1.80 (1.60 to 2.01; 1.72, 1.55 to 1.91, against higher-potency herbal), depression diagnosis 1.34 (1.21 to 1.48; 1.15, 1.03 to 1.25, against higher-potency herbal). US sample of 156: concentrate use and psychosis symptoms r 0.11 (-0.20 to 0.40), anxiety 0.21 (-0.10 to 0.49), depression 0.17 (-0.15 to 0.45). US sample of 191, frequent concentrate against frequent herbal use: anxiety means 1.1 and 0.66, depression 0.72 and 0.76, no significant difference. Within-person survey of 574 people who used cannabis in the past year, mostly infrequently: psychosis-like experiences mean 1.1 with concentrates and 1.2 with herbal cannabis (0 to 10 scale; Cohen's d 0.12). 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders, liquid or resin against dry herbal cannabis: residual or late-onset psychotic disorder odds ratio 0.212 (0.061 to 0.735), which Table 1 labels no association.

evidence_add.extracted: Anxiety, four cross-sectional studies (one fair): generalised anxiety disorder more likely with higher-potency use in a UK sample of 1,087 aged about 24 (odds ratio 1.92, 1.11 to 3.32; adjusted for sex, childhood socio-economic position, depression score at 13 and frequency; rated fair); no difference between higher- and lower-potency herbal cannabis in the 20-country survey (1.05, 0.98 to 1.12). Depression, four cross-sectional studies (one fair): a slight increase in the 20-country survey (higher- against lower-potency herbal 1.18, 1.11 to 1.25) and little evidence in the UK sample (1.28, 0.68 to 2.32). Studies of people using medical cannabis (four for anxiety, one rated fair; three for depression, all poor) gave varied results that the authors call hard to interpret. The authors conclude there is some evidence for anxiety and little for depression.

Most studies took potency from self-reported product type, an approximate proxy for THC content, and none accounted for THC intake as opposed to content; the authors argue that titration, which evidence suggests is partial, would be expected to weaken rather than inflate associations. Some studies compared higher with lower potency directly and others each with no use, so the contrast can be read only within each study. Cross-sectional designs cannot establish direction: people with poorer mental health might choose higher-potency cannabis as self-medication. There is no agreement on confounders; amount used was adjusted for in only one study; frequency was a covariate in some studies and part of a combined potency-and-frequency variable in others, and may be a confounder or a mediator.
